extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mass communication, journalism, and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating patterns and standards of news/media content (bias, representation, newsworthiness, sourcing, geographic and demographic coverage) as discussed in an academic textbook on media sociology. Useful for content analysts, journalism scholars, and students studying how news is selected and framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology / Selection Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The deliberate selection of topics (or parts of the country) that are considered newsworthy; ideology includes unintended yet hidden bias that is 'embedded in texts' (p. 194).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficult to demonstrate with simple content analysis because enumeration of selected items does not necessarily reveal underlying ideology; selection itself can bestow importance as much as reflect it (Cook, p.57). Look for patterns in what is chosen or omitted rather than only counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether reporting is fair and objective — whether reporters avoid value statements and direct assertions, making mostly factual inferences about events (Robinson & Sheehan, 1983).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical research often gives news media good marks for fairness; examine frequency of value-laden statements, direct assertions about actors, and reliance on inference versus fact. Note that apparent objectivity can coexist with selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of Minority Groups / Media Power Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether key media form 'a closely knit media power structure' in which minority groups and concerns are not well represented (Altschull, 1990, p. 330).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence, prominence, and roles of minority actors; check for underrepresentation and marginalization across beats and outlets. Consider institutional gatekeeping decisions that limit minority visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Balance vs Events-Driven Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures (equal column inches, seconds of airtime) are a simplistic standard for fairness; if events drive news, equal measure is not necessarily appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists/watchdogs often use ruler-and-stopwatch measures, but analysts should account for event occurrence rates — quantitative balance can misrepresent fairness when events are not evenly distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse-Race / Symbolic Coverage over Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Predominant focus on 'who is ahead' in contests (horse race) and on symbolic events rather than substantive issue-oriented coverage (e.g., more on campaign standing or symbolic acts than policy positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count and compare stories about standings/symbols versus issue-focused reporting; examples include disproportionate coverage of symbolic visits or TV appearances (Kaniss 1991; Graff on Clinton's Arsenio appearance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity Toward Front-Runners and Incumbents
rubrics_metrics.description: News coverage can be systematically negative toward front-runners and incumbents, with coverage becoming more favorable for those who drop out (Robinson, 1981).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze tone and critical framing relative to candidate status (front-runner/incumbent vs challenger); look for consistent patterns of critique versus magnanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance as a Newsworthiness Criterion (Statistical and Normative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The media tell what is normal by showing what is deviant; statistically deviant (unusual) and normative deviant (breaking norms/laws) events are more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify stories selected because they are surprising/rare ('Boy sees dad die at mom's grave') or norm-breaking (salacious rape details, cult behavior). Note that as events become common (e.g., medical procedures), they lose newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and Framing of Deviant Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage often emphasizes deviance of groups (e.g., describing Branch Davidians as a 'secretive religious cult'), focusing on appearance and criminality rather than message and giving more attention to official viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for condescending tone, emphasis on appearance over message, reliance on official sources (police, attorneys), camera perspectives favoring authorities; such framing restricts diversity of political discourse (Hertog & McLeod, 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence Prevalence and News Preference for Violent Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: High incidence of violence on television relative to real life; news shows prefer violent crime over nonviolent crimes, and deaths due to violence are more likely to be reported than deaths due to disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure violent acts per hour/character involvement (Gerbner et al. findings); in news, assess whether violent crimes receive disproportionate coverage compared to their real-world frequency (Combs & Slovic; various content analyses). Consider programming and commercial promos as sources of televised violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual Content Frequency and Portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual acts occur with measurable frequency in prime time TV, often depicted between unmarried people and not reflective of real-life distributions (Greenberg et al., 1980).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record frequency and context of sexual behavior portrayal; note demographic patterns and normative implications; fewer studies exist but assess comparability to reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping and Distorted Portrayals (Mental Illness, Ethnic Groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media frequently present distorted pictures (e.g., mentally ill portrayed as dangerous; pervasive ethnic stereotypes of American Indians, Asians, Latinos, African Americans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine deviation from expert opinion or public belief (Nunnaly, 1981); look for emphasis on bizarre symptoms, association with criminality, occupational/status stereotyping (Signorielli, Greenberg). Document recurring stereotypic images and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source Dominance and Source-Controlled Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: News sources are dominated by officials; many stories originate through routine, source-controlled channels (official proceedings, press conferences, press releases) with government and corporate sources heavily represented (Sigal; Daley & O'Neill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proportion of stories using government/industry sources; evaluate diversity of voices and presence (or absence) of dissenting actors; consider implications for legitimation of particular positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Selection Emphasizing Official and Deviant Activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Major activities in the news are government conflicts and disagreements, decisions/proposals/ceremonies, protests, crimes, scandals, investigations, and disasters—i.e., official or deviant events (Gans, 1979).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize beats/topics and compare prominence of official/deviant activities versus routine social/institutional issues; measure initiation of subjects by candidates/actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Representativeness (Coast and Beltway Bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneven geographic distribution of coverage: Pacific Coast and Northeast overcovered; Midwest undercovered; 'beltway bias' with Washington stories disproportionately represented (Dominick; Graber; Ryan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare state-by-state story counts to population/electoral metrics; identify concentration on coasts and Washington, D.C.; note entertainment 'hometowns' concentration in big cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Coverage Bias (Crisis Orientation and U.S.-Centricity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign news concentrates on stories relevant to Americans/U.S. interests, with third-world coverage focused on crises (war, terrorism, coups) and developed countries overrepresented relative to population (Larson; Gans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure proportion of international stories that are crisis-oriented; check whether coverage prioritizes U.S.-relevant angles, allies and communist-bloc countries; examine photographic and topic emphasis on conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing of Events (Accident vs Systemic Explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The way media frame events (e.g., Exxon Valdez as an 'accident' rather than evidence of systemic problems) shapes public understanding and can privilege certain institutional narratives (Daley & O'Neill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze dominant explanatory frames in coverage (individual/accidental vs systemic/structural) and the balance of industry/government perspectives versus other analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of International Reporting / Parachute Journalism vs On-the-Ground Correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction in foreign correspondents leads to 'parachute journalism'—quickly assembled reports from wherever the news is—while outlets like CNN can transmit competing national claims globally and broaden voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess number of foreign correspondents and reliance on transient reporting; evaluate depth, context, and multiplicity of international perspectives; consider effects of 24-hour networks on source diversity and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Appeal ('Sizzle') as a Determinant of Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that 'stir the emotions' or have 'sizzle' (disasters, dramatic issues) are more likely to be covered and to receive prominent play than nonemotional but socially significant issues (FitzSimon; Shoemaker et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence of emotionally charged elements and their influence on prominence and frequency of coverage; compare coverage of high-sizzle issues (global warming) to lower-sizzle but important issues (garbage/sludge).
